title: Water Margin
subtitle: Enforcing the Way of Heaven · One Hundred and Eight Heroes Gather at Liangshan
description: Water Margin is China's first full-length novel written in vernacular Chinese, created by the late Yuan and early Ming novelist Shi Nai'an, and is one of the Four Great Classical Novels of Chinese literature. Set in the closing years of the Northern Song dynasty, it tells the tragic tale of one hundred and eight heroes led by Song Jiang, who are forced to flee to Mount Liangshan, gather as sworn brothers, rebel against corrupt authority, and ultimately accept imperial amnesty to campaign against Fang La. Its theme of "officials driving the people to rebellion" and its vivid cast of characters make it an immortal masterpiece of the common people's spirit in Chinese literary history.

route.title: Water Margin: A Cry of Outrage at Injustice — When the Time Comes, Strike
route.intro:
From eight directions they shared one land, though born of different clans they were one family. Heaven and earth revealed the essence of valor and justice; the human realm blended with the heroic and the beautiful. Men from a thousand li apart met face to face each day; one inch of heart could be shared in life and death.
Shi Nai'an (c. 1296–1370), given name Zi'an, style name Nai'an, was a native of Xinghua in Taizhou. He served as an adviser in Zhang Shicheng's rebel army, experiencing firsthand the blood and fire of the late Yuan uprisings, and forged those experiences into the story of Water Margin. The one hundred and eight heroes he created include a drill instructor, a minor clerk, a fisherman, a butcher — ordinary men from the lowest ranks of society, forced to rebel because they had no way out. Let us follow the heroes' footsteps — from the eight-hundred-li marsh of Liangshan to the Eastern Capital Kaifeng, from the tiger-slaying at Jingyang Ridge to Liuhe Pagoda in Hangzhou — and visit the national heritage sites that bear witness to the heroes' gathering, their loyal bonds, and their tragic fate.

stops.title: Stop One: The Liangshan Marsh · Brotherhood Before the Loyalty Hall
stops.content: The eight-hundred-li marsh of Liangshan stretched vast and majestic, reeds and rushes hiding a forest of masts. The Liangshan heroes raised the golden banner of "Enforcing the Way of Heaven" and assembled in the Loyalty Hall. Lin Chong killing Wang Lun by fire, Chao Gai's clever seizure of the Birthday Convoy, Song Jiang's rebellious poem on the wall of Xunyang Pavilion — one brilliant story after another unfolded here. The thirty-six Heavenly Spirits and seventy-two Earthly Fiends swore blood oaths before the Loyalty Hall, entrusting one another with life and death. At the foot of Liangshan, the Qinggudui Site is an elevated mound of cultural accumulation stretching from the Longshan culture through the Shang and Zhou dynasties. Though Liangshan's marshes have long since dried into fertile farmland, standing on this high ground and gazing in all directions, you can still imagine the war ships threading through the reeds and gallant horsemen racing across the landscape. The wind howls over the mountain, as if the war cries of the one hundred and eight heroes still echo in the air. Liangshan itself is not a tall mountain — the main peak rises only 197.9 meters above sea level — but "a mountain need not be high to be famed for its immortals." With Shi Nai'an's pen, Liangshan became one of the most towering peaks in the Chinese heart. Approaching the foot of Liangshan by car, the first thing you see is the three characters "水浒寨" (Water Margin Stronghold) carved above the mountain gate. Climbing the steps, you encounter the Loyalty Hall, Song Jiang's Well, Black Wind Pass, and the Gold-Breaking Pavilion — every name has its counterpart in Water Margin. Black Wind Pass was the stronghold guarded by Li Kui; the wind howls through the gorge like the whistling of Li Kui's twin battle-axes cleaving the air. Standing before the Loyalty Hall and looking down, the once-eight-hundred-li marsh has become a rolling plain of wheat — but close your eyes, and the rustle of reeds, the thrum of war drums, the shouts of the one hundred and eight heroes surge up from the earth. Shi Nai'an wrote Song Jiang crying out in the Loyalty Hall: "Today we one hundred and eight men, in accord with Heaven above and the hearts of men below, live as one and die as one, never betraying one another!" These words, after a thousand years, still set the blood boiling. About thirty kilometers west of Liangshan lies another historical site — the Jiaxiang Wu Family Tomb Carvings. These Han-dynasty stone reliefs are filled with legends of ancient heroes and assassins — Jing Ke's attempt on the King of Qin, Zhuan Zhu's assassination of King Liao, Nie Zheng's assassination of Han Gui — the spirit of "a scholar dies for his knowing patron" stretches from the Han to the Song, from stone to paper. The chivalrous genes of the Liangshan heroes were carved long ago into the deepest cultural memory of this land. Liangshan is not tall, the lake is not deep, but the heroic spirit has never died in a thousand years — that is the secret of Water Margin's immortality.

stops.title: Stop Two: The Great Xiangguo Temple in the Eastern Capital · Lu Zhishen Uproots the Willow Tree
stops.content: After killing the bully Zhen Guanxi with three punches, the Big Monk Lu Zhishen was ordained at Mount Wutai and then dispatched by the abbot to oversee the vegetable garden at the Great Xiangguo Temple in the Eastern Capital. A gang of local ruffians tried to intimidate him, only to be kicked head-first into the cesspool. As the gang acknowledged his superiority, a crow cawed noisily from a willow tree outside the wall. Lu Zhishen strode over, wrapped his arms around the trunk, and with a mighty heave of his torso — "Up!" — uprooted the bowl-thick weeping willow, roots and all! That single pull created one of the most electrifying scenes in Water Margin. Today the Xiangguo Temple in Kaifeng still thrives with incense smoke. This thousand-year-old temple was originally the residence of Lord Xinling of the Warring States period and was already a famous temple under the Tang dynasty. In the Song dynasty, the Great Xiangguo Temple was even more lively, hosting massive markets five times a month where people of every trade and rank gathered — it was amid this bustling city clamor that Lu Zhishen performed his legendary willow-uprooting feat. Standing within the temple and looking up at the ancient eaves, you can almost hear that earth-shaking roar. The Xiangguo Temple was built in the sixth year of Tianbao, Northern Qi (555 AD), and originally called Jianguo Temple. Emperor Ruizong of Tang, Li Dan, bestowed the name Great Xiangguo Temple to commemorate his succession from the title of Prince Xiang. Today the temple's Heavenly King Hall, Great Buddha Hall, Octagonal Glazed Tile Hall, and Sutra Library line up along the central axis. The most stunning sight is the four-faced Thousand-Armed, Thousand-Eyed Guanyin statue in the Octagonal Glazed Tile Hall — carved from a single ginkgo tree, about seven meters tall, with one thousand and forty-eight hands spreading like a peacock's tail, each palm bearing an eye — simultaneously compassionate and awe-inspiring. Looking up at it, a thousand hands seem to reach toward you, a thousand eyes seem to gaze upon you — just like Lu Zhishen's willow-uprooting, overwhelming you with a superhuman power beyond mortal strength. Kaifeng city in the Song dynasty was the largest metropolis in the world at the time, with a population exceeding one million. Lu Zhishen's daily life in the Xiangguo Temple vegetable garden is the perfect intersection of the Water Margin heroes and the common city life — right next to the vegetable patch was the bustling "ten thousand trades" market, where Wu Dalang sold flatbread and young Yun Ge sold pears, all scraping out a living. Walk less than two li north from the Great Xiangguo Temple and you reach the Youguo Temple Pagoda (Kaifeng Iron Pagoda), a glazed brick pagoda built in the first year of Huangyou, Northern Song (1049 AD), 55.88 meters tall, its brown glazed bricks looking like rusted iron from a distance — if Lu Zhishen had looked north from the Xiangguo Temple vegetable garden, he would have seen this pagoda standing tall for over nine hundred years. A temple, a pagoda — the Xiangguo Temple houses the wildest monk in Water Margin; the Iron Pagoda witnessed Kaifeng's most glorious dream.

stops.title: Stop Three: Jingyang Ridge · Wu Song Kills the Tiger
stops.content: On his way home to visit his elder brother, Wu Song passed through Jingyang Ridge in Yanggu County. At the foot of the ridge, he downed eighteen bowls of the inn's famous "three-bowl-and-you-can't-cross-the-ridge" wine. The innkeeper warned him of a man-eating tiger in the hills, but Wu Song thought it was a trick to keep guests. Once on the ridge, the wine hit him, and he lay down on a slab of blue stone to sleep. Suddenly the tiger appeared — Wu Song's intoxication vanished. Bare-handed, he wrestled the beast, pinned it to the ground, and rained down blows like a hailstorm, beating the massive striped creature to death with his fists! From that day on, the "Tiger-Slaying Hero" was famous throughout the land. The Jingyang Ridge Site in Yanggu County is not merely the setting of a legend — buried beneath its soil lies a genuine Longshan-culture ancient city! A prehistoric city and a literary legend meet here in a wondrous encounter that creates an unparalleled cultural landscape. Standing on the ridge, the trees are thick, the mountain wind blows, and you can almost feel the heart-stopping intensity of Wu Song's struggle with the tiger. The archaeological finds at the Jingyang Ridge Site astonished the scholarly world — it is a Longshan-culture ancient city covering about 350,000 square meters, dating back roughly 4,500 years. The city walls were built of rammed earth, the remaining sections still three to four meters high; within the city are large rammed-earth platforms, possibly palace or sacrificial remains. Standing at the edge of the site, the rammed earth from 4,500 years ago beneath your feet, the wind rustling through the poplar trees overhead — the "big worm" of Jingyang Ridge is long extinct, but the existence of this ancient city reminds us that while Wu Song's story may not be historical fact, it grew out of this real and ancient land. Shi Nai'an perhaps never knew that a Longshan city lay buried underground, but the Wu Song he wrote — the strongman who drank eighteen bowls of wine and killed a man-eating tiger bare-handed — represents, like this ancient city, a primal force confronting the wilderness and conquering nature. The wind on Jingyang Ridge howls fiercely; the pine trees roar like a tiger. At the top of the ridge stands a stone tablet bearing five characters: "武松打虎处" (The Place Where Wu Song Killed the Tiger). Looking downhill from the tablet, the slope is not steep; a few gnarled locust trees lean over the path. You can imagine Wu Song rolling up from the blue stone, his drunken eyes making out a striped, white-browed beast bursting from the thicket, its tail cracking through the underbrush — in that instant, his intoxication vanished, every pore on his body exploded. Shi Nai'an wrote: "Wu Song pressed the beast's mouth straight down into the yellow mud pit. The beast, worn out by Wu Song's handling, had no strength left... Wu Song gripped the loose skin on the back of its neck tightly with his left hand, freed his right hand, raised his fist like an iron hammer, and struck with all the strength of his life, blow after blow." This passage sends the adrenaline surging — and all of it happened on this seemingly ordinary yellow-earth ridge. Standing atop Jingyang Ridge, you understand: true heroes are not those who perform on a stage, but those forced out by the wilderness.

stops.title: Stop Four: Dai Temple · Offering Sacrifice to Heaven Before the Tiankuang Hall
stops.content: Though the Water Margin heroes gathered at Liangshan, their fate was always intertwined with Mount Tai. Yan Qing once ascended Mount Tai to challenge the champion wrestler Ren Yuan at a tournament, using his "dove-spin" technique to hurl the "Pillar of Heaven" to the ground, spreading Liangshan's fame across the land. And Mount Tai, where emperors performed the fengshan sacrifices, with its grand and majestic aura, appears repeatedly in the novel. At the foot of Mount Tai, the Dai Temple was where successive emperors stayed before performing the fengshan ceremonies, built in the style of a royal palace. The massive mural inside the Tiankuang Hall, "The God of Mount Tai Sets Out and Returns in Procession," is magnificent in scale — from Qin-Han through Ming-Qing, fengshan ceremonies were performed here again and again. Standing before the hall and looking up at the summit of Mount Tai through swirling clouds and mist, you can almost see Yan Qing's agile form leaping and tumbling on the high platform — the heroic spirit of Liangshan's outlaws and the majesty of the supreme of the Five Sacred Mountains shine together in this place. The Dai Temple was first built in the Han dynasty, covering a total area of 96,000 square meters, making it the largest and most complete ancient building complex on Mount Tai. Passing through Zhengyang Gate, the Yaocan Pavilion, Tiankuang Hall, and Rear Bedchamber unfold along the central axis in sequence, flanked by the Han Cypress Court and Tang Locust Court — ancient trees tower overhead, the oldest Han cypress now over two thousand years old, its bark like iron, its branches twisted and gnarled. The Tiankuang Hall is nine bays wide and four bays deep, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof covered in yellow glazed tiles that glitter gold in the sunlight. The murals on the east, west, and north walls of the hall — "The God of Mount Tai Sets Out and Returns in Procession" — rise 3.3 meters high and stretch 62 meters long, depicting the grand spectacle of the god of Mount Tai's journey: over six hundred figures, more than a hundred horses, dozens of chariots, magnificent in scope — a monumental masterpiece of Song-dynasty mural painting. In Chapter Seventy-Four of Water Margin, "Yan Qing Cleverly Topples the Pillar of Heaven," it was before this very Dai Temple that Yan Qing displayed his prowess on the wrestling platform. Ren Yuan, ten feet tall and calling himself "Pillar of Heaven," had maintained his challenge platform in Tai'an for two years without defeat. Yan Qing, carrying only a crossbow and a bag of silver, traveled from Liangshan to Tai'an. On the platform, Ren Yuan attacked like a hungry tiger, but Yan Qing used his "dove-spin" technique — twisting his body, slipping between Ren Yuan's legs, then driving his shoulder upward — Ren Yuan crashed to the ground and rolled off the platform. The crowd roared like a tidal wave; Liangshan's prestige spread across the whole of Qilu from that day on. Standing before the Tiankuang Hall of Dai Temple, looking up at Mount Tai, you understand why the Water Margin heroes ultimately turned their gaze here — Liangshan could be a place to gather, but only Mount Tai could "enfeoff" gods. From gathering to amnesty, from rebellion to surrender — the tragedy of Water Margin lies hidden between this mountain and this temple.

stops.title: Stop Five: Jinan Prefecture · Heroes' Shadows by Daming Lake
stops.content: Jinan is an important stage in the Water Margin story. After the great battle at Qingzhou involving Qin Ming, Hua Rong, and Huang Xin, Song Jiang led his army eastward, and Jinan Prefecture became a strategic stronghold. The novel depicts Jinan with its seventy-two gushing springs, the misty waves of Daming Lake, and the pine forests of Thousand Buddha Mountain — "lotus on four sides, willows on three; a city of mountain hues half filled with lake." The Lingyan Temple in Changqing District, Jinan, is one of the four great temples of China. First built in the Eastern Jin dynasty, it flourished in the Tang and Song. The forty Song-dynasty polychrome arhat statues in the Thousand Buddha Hall were hailed by Liang Qichao as "the finest sculptures within the seas." These arhats, some deep in thought, some with glaring eyes, each with a distinct expression — one cannot help wondering whether Shi Nai'an drew inspiration from these vivid arhat figures when conceiving the one hundred and eight heroes of Water Margin. Every character is brimming with life, just like these clay sculptures, still living in people's hearts across a thousand years. The Lingyan Temple sits at the foot of Fangshan Mountain on the northwestern flank of Mount Tai. The name "Lingyan" (Spirit Rock) comes from the legend of the Eastern Jin monk Lang Gong preaching here, causing "fierce beasts to submit and the mountain crags to nod." The temple's Pizhi Pagoda, 55.7 meters tall, is an octagonal nine-story dense-eave brick pagoda built in the fifth year of Chunhua, Northern Song (994 AD), decorated with reliefs of vajra warriors and flying apsaras. The Thousand Buddha Hall is the soul of Lingyan Temple — at its center, three great Buddhas are enshrined: Vairocana (the Dharmakaya), Locana (the Sambhogakaya), and Shakyamuni (the Nirmanakaya). Behind the great Buddhas, the walls are covered with countless small cast-bronze Buddhas, layer upon layer, glittering gold like a sea of stars. But what truly takes your breath away is not the Buddhas, but the forty Song-dynasty polychrome arhat statues ranged around three sides of the hall. These arhats stand about 1.55 to 1.6 meters tall — slightly larger than life. Some knit their brows in deep thought, some open their mouths as if debating, some press their palms together, some lower their eyes in meditation. Each one's facial expression is entirely unique: one bulges with veins as if subduing a dragon, another's mouth turns up faintly as if sharing a knowing insight, another's eyes hold compassion as if beholding the suffering of all beings. The clay bodies are covered with polychrome painting; the texture of skin, the folds of robes, the spirit of brows and eyes — all reach the pinnacle of the art. Liang Qichao lingered here in admiration and wrote the inscription "the finest sculptures within the seas." Standing among these arhats, you cannot help but think of the one hundred and eight heroes of Shi Nai'an's Water Margin — those outlaws from every walk of life, did they not each, through their own unique "appearance" — glowering Li Kui, cool-smiling Wu Yong, simple-hearted Lu Zhishen — live out the same character of "righteousness"? Jinan's seventy-two springs gush day and night; Lingyan Temple's bell tones pierce the woods and cross the waters. Water Margin is not merely a story of rebellion; it is a collective portrait of the Chinese soul.

stops.title: Stop Six: Liuhe Pagoda in Hangzhou · Attaining Perfection by the Sound of the Tide
stops.content: After the Liangshan heroes accepted imperial amnesty and campaigned against Fang La in the south, most were killed or wounded. Wu Song lost an arm in battle. After the war, he did not return to the capital with Song Jiang but chose to become a monk at Liuhe Temple in Hangzhou, living out his days there. On the day the army returned in triumph, the Qiantang River tide surged with a thunderous roar — Wu Song sat beneath the pagoda listening to the tide, his face serene. Gone was the ferocity of his tiger-slaying, gone the bold swagger of his drunken beating of Jiang the Gate God of Hell. What remained was only the desolate calm of one who had seen everything. The Liuhe Pagoda on Moon-Wheel Mountain by the Qiantang River was first built in the Northern Song dynasty to calm the river's tidal bore. The brick pagoda core preserves Southern Song structure — eight sides, seven stories — standing tall and imposing. From the top, looking out over the Qiantang River, the water meets the sky, the tide rises and falls. A tiger-slaying hero here laid down his weapons and his obsessions. This is perhaps the deepest ending of Water Margin: not a hero's death on the battlefield, but the return to stillness. The Liuhe Pagoda was first built in the third year of Kaibao, Northern Song (970 AD), by Qian Hongchu, King of Wuyue, to control the tidal bore. The pagoda stands 59.89 meters tall, with thirteen visible stories and seven internal levels — its "seven bright, six dark" structure is exquisitely ingenious. The octagonal body has a teapot-door entrance on each side leading to the core. Ascending level by level, the view changes at every story: at level one, the river is like a silk ribbon; level two, the mountains undulate; level three, the city profile emerges... At the top level, the entire Qiantang River spreads out below — the broad channel, boats like leaves, the river wind whipping your robes. One hundred and four bronze bells hang from the eaves, their ding-dong sound rising and falling in the wind like Sanskrit chanting, like the sound of the tide, like time itself flowing. The final chapter of Water Margin describes Wu Song's end briefly and poignantly: "From then on, Wu Song took holy orders at Liuhe Temple, and lived to the age of eighty before passing away." The strongman who killed a man-eating tiger bare-handed on Jingyang Ridge, the hero who drunkenly beat Jiang the Gate God and raised havoc at Feiyun Ford, finally chose a pagoda and a river tide. Shi Nai'an did not write what Wu Song thought about in the pagoda, but we can imagine: he must have stood countless times at the top of Liuhe Pagoda looking out over the Qiantang River. The tide came in like ten thousand galloping horses; it receded like a beauty's sigh. Wu Song lost an arm, but he let go of much more — hatred, glory, obsession — all came and went with the tide. The sound of the Qiantang tide beneath Liuhe Pagoda has never ceased in a thousand years. It is the desolation of a hero's end — and the stillness of a hero's awakening. This pagoda is not just a building; it is the deepest full stop of the entire Water Margin.
